title: Reforming medical device regulation in Europe: centralization, governance, and the case for an EU medical device agency

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:
《Reforming medical device regulation in Europe: centralization, governance, and the case for an EU medical device agency》：研究问题的原文依据。

【A complex web: how the current European MedTech system operates · p0020】Accompanied by a recent broader shift among European legislators to reduce regulatory burdens and harmonise digital regulations (the Digital Omnibus package8 and the Digital Fitness Check9), the European Commission published a proposal for simplifying MDR and IVDR on December 16, 2025.10 The proposal, which will probably come into force in 2027 once it has passed through the legislative consultation and refinement process, aims to reduce the regulatory burden, including by strengthening the centralisation of conformity assessment processes, and addressing some of the issues outlined below, particularly those concerning NB (e.g., reducing NB involvement for some device types, reducing unannounced audits and the frequency of audits in general, promoting presubmission dialogue and increasing NB regulation and oversight).

【Safety, evidence, and the risks of regulatory divergence · p0035】It can be hard for innovators to determine what the EUs stance or approval pathway for a particular technology really is. This becomes especially problematic for new medical devices increasingly taking the form of combination technologies. For example, an AI-powered closed-loop insulin delivery system (“artificial pancreas”), falls under multiple product-related regulatory frameworks, such as medicines (insulin), medical devices (the pump and the continuous glucose monitor), and artificial intelligence (the AI predictive dosing algorithm), such systems could also be linked to patient-used IVD-analysing samples of body fluids (e.g., urine). In practice, manufacturers have to comply with each of these regimes when the device falls within scope. Because parts of these frameworks may appear to overlap in practice (e.g., inconsistencies in qualification and classification,26 gaps in interpretation regarding ethical compliance,27 and uncertainties concerning assessment roles and responsibilities28), this can create unclear and often additional requirements for manufacturers,29 as well as slow timelines and conflicting decisions.30 Moreover, regulatory uncertainty is directly connected to increased approval times for innovative and novel medical devices, resulting in additional costs.31 Acknowledging this, the MDCG and the Joint Artificial Intelligence Board (AIB) explicitly provides a structured approach to avoiding duplication and minimising additional burdens.32 Additionally, the Commission’s MDR/IVDR 2.0 proposal together with the proposal for an “European Biotech Act”33 aims to provide a clearer categorization of combined products. However, due to divergent national implementation of the regulatory frameworks, it is particularly important for MedTech manufacturers to have access to dialogue formats during pre-submission stages or to general ad hoc expertise. Unfortunately, scientific or clinical development advice is not/very limited available from decision makers (NB are explicitly restricted to consultancy activities,1 and NCA show divergent practices and knowledge constraints34 (e.g., 57% offer advice prior to application, but only 11% offer national scientific advice beyond clinical-trial aspects35), and a general lack of coordinated early regulatory advice34). In reality, advice is only available from EXPAMED, who have no decision making role in the system. There are no signs of a broader shift in this regard, as recently launched pilot programmes follow the same path, such as EMA’s pilot for “breakthrough” devices36: it offers manufacturers priority scientific advice from EXPAMED, but it does not touch the underlying authorisation architecture, therefore adding layers to the unchanged decentralised system with no control on final decisions made by NB. Other jurisdictions, such as the US, are adopting a more courageous approach by linking centralized binding advice and authorization (FDA’s Breakthrough Devices Program) with centralized reimbursement (the newly proposed RAPID Coverage Pathway, which would issue a proposed national coverage determination the same day a breakthrough device receives FDA authorisation)37 - something that is currently unthinkable within the multiple layers of overlapping EU decentralization.

sections.title: 研究方法
sections.text:
《Reforming medical device regulation in Europe: centralization, governance, and the case for an EU medical device agency》：方法与研究设计的原文依据。

【A complex web: how the current European MedTech system operates · p0010】Medical Technologies are essential for delivering healthcare, as they enable the diagnosis, prevention, monitoring, prediction, treatment or alleviation of diseases, disabilities or injuries.1 While their use as a hardware device, in-vitro diagnostic device or digital tools/software is accompanied by inherent risks that can result in patient harm, they are covered by comprehensive regulatory frameworks. In Europe, MedTech products are primarily governed by the Medical Device Regulation (MDR) 2017/7451 and the In Vitro Diagnostic Medical Device Regulation (IVDR) 2017/746,2 which are based on a risk class system according to their potential impact on patients and users. Prior to market approval, manufacturers must demonstrate that the MDR/IVDR requirements have been met based on conformity assessment. For certain devices, this procedure involves designated third-party entities (Notified Bodies (NB)). On completion, manufacturers can apply the CE marking, which is currently valid in over 100 jurisdictions around the world.3

【Safety, evidence, and the risks of regulatory divergence · p0025】According to the theory of system competition, companies choose their preferred market much like consumers picking between competing products,11 pursuing market access in regulatory frameworks considered optimal.12 An optimal condition would be to have well-functioning, self-balancing regulatory systems that safeguards patient safety, promotes responsible, technologically-led improvements in healthcare delivery, and enables and sustains a homegrown technology and industrial sector. Such an ecosystem strengthens health systems and, via economic growth and employment, helps generate the revenues that ultimately finance care. In international comparison, it is evident that Europe is losing ground here. For instance, according to a representative survey among 211 medical device and IVD manufacturers conducted in 2024,3 they deprioritize the EU as their first regulatory market. The results show that the number of new innovative product launches in the EU has dropped by 33% for large medical device manufacturers and by 19% for small ones, as well as by 40% for large and by 12% for small IVD manufacturers. Meanwhile, the US market is gaining in popularity, particularly among large manufacturers. This is accompanied by a significant decline in innovation activities, especially concerning the development of new devices (59% of IVD and 54,4% of medical device manufacturers) within SMEs.3

sections.title: 主要结果
sections.text:
《Reforming medical device regulation in Europe: centralization, governance, and the case for an EU medical device agency》：结果的原文依据；数值与适用人群以引文为准。

【Conclusion · p0125】The importance of appropriate and effective regulation of medical devices is indisputable. Internationally, the growing adoption of AI-enabled technologies is likely to be among the most consequential trends in health over the next decade.83 However, the EU has been too long flying blind, with an intransparent and fragmented approach to addressing critical new technology advances, providing limited support to EU MedTech through this period of change. By introducing the Digital Omnibus package as well as the proposed MDR and IVDR revision in December 2025, European legislators recognized that technical sovereignty and competitiveness required changes. The remaining question is how to translate that recognition into a governance structure that delivers increased efficiency while still protecting fundamental European values and rights. Whether the EU retains the current regulatory governance structure, adopts a mixed centralised/decentralised model, or creates the most centralised medical device regulator model possible within EU-system, it must get the regulatory system to work in a coordinated manner. This would be most straightforward to achieve through a highly centralised approach. If the EU instead adopts a partially decentralised “half-way-house”, the best available path is to be aware of the model’s weaknesses and to limit their effects by taking account of approaches we suggest as the best hope for EU MedTech and provision of much needed innovations to the EU healthcare sector.

【Conclusion · p0130】References for this Health Policy were identified through searches of Google Scholar and PubMed with the search terms “EU medical device regulation reform”, “centralization EU regulatory governance”, “decentralization EU regulatory governance”, “digital health regulation EU”, “European agencies legitimation”, “central authorisation”, “EU agencies delegation”, “EU agency accountability”, “future governance”, “European political strategy”, “fiscal federalism EU”, “notified bodies medical devices EU”, “FDA medical device approval”, “clinical evaluation consultation procedure”, “clinical evaluation evidence MDR IVDR”, “appropriateness of clinical data MDR”, “complex regulatory systems”, “principal-agent theory decentralization”, “risk-return trade-off centralization”, “regulatory work-sharing”, and “delegation of powers” until January 2026, and via an internet search engine search with Google using the same search terms. Only papers published in English were reviewed. The final reference list was generated on the basis of originality and relevance to the broad scope of this Health Policy.
